passage: The message landed while Indu was waiting for the lift in her Ghaziabad apartment block: "delete ur post abt the bus stop or u will regret it. I know ur tuition time." No profile picture, an account made that day. Her thumb was already typing try me, loser, when she stopped. Her heart was hammering. This wasn't a comment war; whoever it was knew where she would be at six. She deleted the draft, took screenshots of the message and the empty profile, and went straight to Vijay Mama, who was fixing the fan in the living room. He read it twice and climbed down the ladder. "You didn't answer? Good. We don't argue with this." He called her mother, emailed the screenshots to the school principal, and that evening sat with her while they filed a complaint on the police cyber-crime portal. For the next week he walked her to tuition himself.

qa.q: What did the message say it knew?
qa.a: It said it knew her tuition time.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when her thumb started typing 'try me'?
qa.a: Indu felt scared, her heart hammering, and also angry, which pushed her toward a defiant reply; stopping shows the fear and good sense winning over the urge to fight back.

qa.q: Which steps kept Indu safer?
qa.a: She didn't reply, saved screenshots of the message and profile and told Vijay Mama at once; he informed her mother and the principal, filed a complaint that evening and walked her to tuition.

qa.q: How did Vijay Mama read the message?
qa.a: Vijay Mama took it as a real danger rather than a challenge, reading it twice and climbing straight down to act.

grounding: It shows a teenager treating an online threat seriously, not engaging, keeping a record and reporting it to a trusted adult, the school and the authorities.

"Uniforms kill self-expression," Wasim said, slapping the desk. "Forty kids dressed like photocopies. That's not a school, that's a factory."
"Can I answer?" Avni asked.
"You'll say discipline. Everyone says discipline."
"I wasn't going to say discipline."
Mrs Kaur raised a finger. "Wasim, let her finish."
"Fine."
"At my old school there was no uniform," Avni said. "Kids got teased every day for wearing the same two shirts. A uniform hid who could afford what."
The class went quiet. Wasim opened his mouth to laugh, then didn't.
"Okay," he said. "That's a real point. I hadn't thought about money."
"So you agree?"
"No. But maybe the answer isn't no uniform. Maybe it's a simple uniform plus one free-dress day a week, with a rule against teasing."
"That's... actually not bad."
Mrs Kaur wrote both points on the board. "Now that is a debate."

qa.q: What did Avni say happened at her old school?
qa.a: Kids got teased every day for wearing the same two shirts.

qa.q: What might Wasim have felt when he opened his mouth to laugh and didn't?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt caught off guard and a little humbled, since the point about money was new to him; he may also have felt some respect for an argument he hadn't expected.

qa.q: What went wrong at the start, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Wasim tried to win by slapping the desk and predicting Avni's answer; listening, admitting 'That's a real point' and adapting the idea turned it into a real debate.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Wasim said 'Everyone says discipline'?
qa.a: Avni likely felt talked over and brushed off, which is why she had to ask to answer and then correct him.

grounding: It shows a teenager defending a view with claims, slipping into volume and ridicule, then acknowledging a good point and refining the argument.

passage:
"Papa, can we talk about the phone rule? Properly, not shouting."
Anand looked up from the newspaper. "Last time 'properly' ended with a door slam."
"I know. Sorry for that. Here's my idea. Right now the phone goes to the hall at nine. I want it till ten-thirty on school nights."
"And you'll be up till two."
"That's why I'm offering this: at ten-thirty it goes on the hall charger, and I put it there myself. You don't have to ask."
"And if it doesn't?"
"Then it's back to nine, no argument. Two-week trial. You can check the screen-time page every Sunday."
Anand folded the paper. "Why ten-thirty?"
"The group study call goes till ten. I've been missing the last hour, and then sneaking the phone back from the hall to catch up."
"You've been sneaking it?"
"Yes, Papa. I'd rather not have to."
A long pause. "Two weeks. Hall charger. I'm checking on Sundays, Irfan."
"Deal."

qa.q: Till what time does the group study call go?
qa.a: The group study call goes till ten.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when admitting to sneaking the phone?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt nervous and a bit ashamed saying it, but also wanted to be trusted; the admission may also have been a way to show honesty.

qa.q: Which part of Irfan's proposal made it easier to say yes?
qa.a: A clear two-week trial with a built-in consequence, putting the phone on the hall charger unasked and Sunday checks, gave Anand ways to build trust. 👍

qa.q: How might Anand have felt hearing about the sneaking?
qa.a: Anand may have felt surprised and a little hurt, but the honest admission next to a calm plan likely made the trial feel safer to agree to.

grounding: It shows a teenager negotiating phone time with a parent by offering trust-building steps and a trial period instead of arguing or sneaking.

passage:
Dear Dolma Didi,
You told me to write when stuff got weird, so here it is. On Saturday at Karishma's birthday, some of the older girls went up to the terrace with a vape and kept waving it at me. "Just one pull, Ritu, don't be a baby." I said no. Then I tried your trick: "Coach tests our breathing on Monday, I can't." They laughed but backed off for ten minutes. When they started again, I said, "I'm going down for cake, anyone coming?" Nobody came, and my face was hot, but I went. Karishma found me later and said, "Sorry, they're like that. You don't have to go up." She's fine. They're not. They've been messaging me all week calling me boring. Last night I showed Mummy, and she called Karishma's mum straight away. I think I'll sit with the hockey team at lunch for a while.
Love, Ritu

qa.q: What excuse did Ritu give on the terrace?
qa.a: Ritu said Coach tests their breathing on Monday, so Ritu couldn't.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when walking down for cake alone?
qa.a: Ritu felt embarrassed, face hot, yet determined; there may also have been some loneliness, since nobody came along.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's moves helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saying no, using a rule as cover and then leaving for the cake got Ritu away from the pressure; showing Mummy the messages brought in an adult when it kept going.

qa.q: How might Karishma have felt seeing the older girls push Ritu?
qa.a: Karishma likely felt embarrassed about her guests and wanted Ritu to feel okay, so she apologised and said Ritu didn't have to go up.

grounding: It shows a teenager refusing a risky offer by saying no, citing a rule and leaving, a peer accepting the refusal, and repeated pressure being taken to an adult.

passage: Kunal hovered in the kitchen doorway of their Pune flat while Kavitha stirred the dal, twisting the hem of his T-shirt. "Aai, if I tell you something, will you shout first or listen first?" Kavitha turned the flame down. "Listen first. Shouting maybe later." He almost smiled. "We didn't go to Sahil's today. We went to the quarry lake. Sahil slipped on the rocks near the edge. Someone grabbed him, he's okay. But he went under for a second." Kavitha's spoon stopped. Her face went tight, then she breathed out and pulled out a stool. "Sit. Tell me all of it." He did: who went, whose idea it was, how scared he had been. She didn't take his phone or ground him right then. She said, "I'm glad you told me tonight," and called Sahil's mother to check he was really fine. A week later, when a maths test went badly, Kunal told her at the door, before she even asked.

qa.q: Where did they go instead of Sahil's?
qa.a: They went to the quarry lake.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he twisted his T-shirt hem in the doorway?
qa.a: Kunal was nervous and afraid of being shouted at, and probably still shaken about Sahil going under; asking 'shout first or listen first?' shows he wanted to be heard.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that made Kunal likely to tell her again?
qa.a: She promised to listen first, steadied her own face, sat him down to hear everything, thanked him and checked on Sahil instead of punishing on the spot.

qa.q: What was it like for Kavitha to hear about the quarry lake?
qa.a: It frightened her, as her stopped spoon and tight face show, but she chose to breathe and listen so the conversation stayed open.

grounding: It shows a teenager telling a parent about an unsafe outing, and a calm, listening response that makes the next disclosure more likely.

passage:
Tuesday, 1 a.m. After another loud night at home, Sonali typed a long public story: "my parents screamed for 2 hours again, I hate this house, I can't breathe here." She added the name of her street and a photo from her window, and posted it.
Wednesday. By first period, forty people had seen it. Two classmates sent crying faces; an account she didn't know wrote, "dm me, I'll listen 😘". Her stomach dropped. Varun found her near the water cooler. "Hey. I saw your story. You okay? Maybe take the street name down, anyone can see that." She deleted it right there. At lunch they talked on the steps, and he told her the school counsellor had helped him when his parents split up.
The next Monday. Another bad night. Sonali opened the app, typed three lines, stopped, and read them as if she were a stranger. Then she deleted the draft and texted Varun instead. In the morning she knocked on the counsellor's door.

qa.q: How many people had seen the story by first period?
qa.a: Forty people had seen it by first period.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when the unknown account wrote to her?
qa.a: Sonali felt exposed and alarmed, her stomach dropping, as she realised strangers could see her street and feelings; she may also have felt some shame at how public it was.

qa.q: What small step helped Sonali the next Monday?
qa.a: Sonali read the draft as a stranger would, deleted it, texted Varun instead and went to the counsellor in the morning, keeping heavy things with trusted people.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt reading the 1 a.m. story?
qa.a: Varun was probably worried about both Sonali's feelings and her safety, which is why he asked if she was okay and pointed out the street name.

grounding: It shows a teenager posting personal details and feelings publicly in distress, then learning to pause, think about audience and permanence, and turn to trusted people instead.

passage: In the girls' hostel study hall, Rajni waited until Rekha sat down with her basketball bag before saying, lightly, "Oh, you still remember what my face looks like?" She laughed as she said it, eyes on her notebook. It was the same kind of line she had tried on Pinky last month, about something else, and Pinky had repeated it down the whole corridor as a joke. So this time Rajni watched closely. Rekha didn't laugh. She put her bag down. "Is that a joke or a real one?" Rajni shrugged. "Half." "I've been at practice every evening," Rekha said. "I thought you didn't mind. Walk to dinner together, at least?" Rajni's shoulders came down a little. On the walk she said the other half: that she had felt left behind since the team started, and silly for feeling it. Rekha linked arms with her. "Not silly. Tell me sooner next time."

qa.q: Where did Rajni say the line to Rekha?
qa.a: Rajni said it in the girls' hostel study hall.

qa.q: Why did Rajni say it with a laugh and her eyes on her notebook?
qa.a: Rajni was testing whether it was safe to show she felt left behind and hurt; after Pinky mocked her last month she was probably wary, so the joke protected her.

qa.q: What makes Rekha a safer person to share with than Pinky?
qa.a: Rekha stopped, asked whether it was a joke or real, and offered to walk to dinner, showing care, while Pinky had turned a hint into corridor gossip. 🤍

qa.q: How did Rekha see the evenings at practice before Rajni spoke?
qa.a: Rekha thought Rajni didn't mind, so the hint was news, and hearing it helped Rekha make time and ask to be told sooner.

grounding: It shows a teenager half-joking to test the response before revealing a feeling, and sharing fully only with someone who has shown care.

Dear Rehana,
The group chat misses you, and so do I. We still call ourselves the Back Bench Pakoras and still reply to everything with "as per the prophecy", which makes no sense to anyone but us, and that's the whole point. I wanted to tell you something, because you'd have had an opinion. On Monday a new girl, Meenal, sat with us at lunch and we did the full pakora routine. She kept laughing half a second late, looking from face to face. Then Anu did the voice, the one copying Mr Das's stammer, and everyone cracked up, and I laughed too. Meenal didn't. She went quiet and left early. Later I found out her brother stammers. I felt sick. On Tuesday I explained the prophecy joke to her from the start, and told Anu the voice has to go. Anu sulked for a day. Meenal is in the chat now.
Miss your terrible puns,
Sudha

qa.a: They called themselves the Back Bench Pakoras.

qa.a: Sudha felt sick with guilt and shame for laughing at the stammer voice; there may also have been worry about how Meenal now saw the whole group.

qa.q: Which choices on Tuesday helped, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the prophecy joke let Meenal into the in-group, and telling Anu the voice has to go stopped a joke built on someone's pain.

qa.a: Meenal laughed half a second late, looking from face to face, so the private jokes left her outside; the stammer voice then hurt, and she left early.

passage: Last term I became briefly famous for a meme. The canteen had raised samosa prices again, so I edited a picture of a school circular to say "Samosas now available on monthly instalment plan." I posted it in the class group and it spread through three batches by lunch. People loved it because it said what everyone felt without a speech. Then two things happened. A Class 7 parent phoned the office asking about the instalment plan; they'd thought it was real. And someone replied with their own version mocking Raju bhaiya, who runs the counter and walks with a limp. Aadhya messaged me: "Simran, yours was funny. That one isn't. He'll see it." My face went hot. I asked the group to delete the reply, and I added "SATIRE, not a real circular" to mine. Next day I bought two samosas at the new price and said sorry to Raju bhaiya anyway.

qa.q: What did Simran's meme say about samosas?
qa.a: It said samosas were now available on monthly instalment plan.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Aadhya's message arrived?
qa.a: Simran felt embarrassed and uneasy, face going hot, seeing the joke had led to something hurtful; there may also have been a sting that the satire was taken as fact.

qa.q: What did Simran do to limit the harm?
qa.a: Simran asked the group to delete the mocking reply, labelled the meme as satire, and apologised to Raju bhaiya in person.

qa.q: How might Raju bhaiya be affected by the reply meme?
qa.a: Being mocked for a limp in front of the students Raju bhaiya serves every day could feel humiliating, which is why Aadhya warned the meme would be seen.

grounding: It shows a teenager's satirical meme carrying a shared attitude, then being mistaken for fact and followed by a reply that mocks a vulnerable person.
